title: The Brain Rot cinematic universe: John Pork vs Bombardiro Crocodilo
content:
The following is a deeply reported look into a growing phenomenon on Instagram Reels. To unlock more of my deep dives into emerging online spaces and internet trends, and to keep this newsletter alive, become a paid subscriber today.

I cannot produce this newsletter without your financial support! Your money goes directly towards reporting costs.

Right now, there's an epic story playing out across Instagram Reels. John Pork, a virtual influencer with a pig's head on a human body, was allegedly murdered by Tim Cheese, an AI-generated rat who was once Pork's best friend. The murder was witnessed by Pingu, the animated penguin who starred in a Swiss children's show in the 90s. Simon Claw, an AI-generated cat, may have aided in the killing, while Marvin Beak, a war-hardened bird and former assassin, was hired to avenge John’s death.

Videos telling this story, piece by piece, are amassing tens of millions of collective views across Instagram Reels. The story has become so popular that it has spurred IRL meetups and marches in Europe. It has expanded into a sprawling, fantastical tale with frequent pivots and cliffhangers. Reels users have developed and introduced a slew of new characters into the John Pork universe, including Tina Cheese, Bob Bacon, and Agent 5.5. Each character has a detailed backstory and role in the larger narrative.

​The rise of John Pork lore, which has recently crossed over into the Italian Brainrot cinematic universe, exemplifies a transformative shift in media, where decentralized, AI-driven storytelling is reshaping the online entertainment landscape.​ Users are leveraging easily-accessible AI image and video generation tools to produce videos, images, and narratives that collectively build out complex stories around different characters to move a plot forward.

This collaborative storytelling approach allows for rapid development and diversification of the narrative, which helps amass a wide audience in the process. While thousands of people contribute constantly to the ever-evolving story, new characters and plot points become canon only as they amass the most views and comments.

Though the John Pork lore is among the most popular content on Reels right now, there is evidence of this trend all across the platform. The proliferation of Italian Brain Rot, for instance, is another example of this character-based collaborative storytelling.

After an AI generated image of a shark wearing blue Nike sneakers went viral, (given the name Tralalero Tralala in Italian), the Italian brain rot cinematic universe expanded to include characters like Bombardiro Crocodilo, a crocodile-faced bomber plane, Lirili Larila, a cactus-elephant hybrid who wears Birkenstocks, Tun Tun Tun Sahur, a wooden man made out of a giant stick who carries a bat, and Brr Brr Patapim, a forest-monkey fusion with oversized feet.

moresquasch1104
A post shared by @moresquasch1104

Users have begun creating intricate back stories to these AI-generated characters, often accompanied by rhyming Italian text-to-speech narrations, and creating new storylines about how the different characters' lives intersect. Lately, all of the Italian brain rot characters have been arrested by the police and engaging in violent behavior.

All of this content falls into the broader online category of brain rot, which is a term that basically means hyper-online content optimized for engagement. While the phrase initially described low effort engagement bait, lately, brain rot content has become more narrative and complex. Content in the broader brain rot genre is now a major force in youth culture and is pushing the boundaries of what entertainment looks like on the internet.

I think it's interesting that John Pork content is dominating on Reels. Though TikTok has always played host to a range of participatory stories, and many of the Italian brain rot characters originally emerged on TikTok, the phenomenon has dominated Reels in large part because of Meta's unabashed embrace of AI-generated content. There also aren't as many creative tools available on Instagram compared to TikTok, making it harder to produce and edit original content. So, users turn to AI.

Mason Kaiser, a 22 year old senior at Elon University in North Carolina, who runs the podcast Reel Talk, where he and his two friends, Carter Puckett and Christian Van Voorhees discuss trending Instagram Reels content, said that the norms on Instagram have also contributed to the AI slop storytelling rise.

"The Instagram Reels community as a whole loves to create storylines for people and whatever they're watching," he said. "I guess that's what makes it so much of a community. I feel like I don't see this stuff on TikTok as much as I do on Reels."

For instance, after a couple of musicians using AI generated animals as their online avatars became popular on Reels, people began creating backstories and lore about them.

There's Civ, an AI generated rapping bear, whose recent St. Patrick's day video amassed millions of views and Wolfie, an AI generated rapping wolf, who also continuously goes viral on Reels. (Wolfie and Civ are now beefing about who was the original viral AI animal rapper and Wolfie is planning to drop a diss track today).

In both cases, a real artist seems to be recording the vocals but performing in an AI costume. When Wolfie and Civ began hitting people's algorithms, it wasn't long before people started inserting them into storylines that crossed over with John Pork and Italian brain rot.

"I think we're in a revolutionary AI period where it's like, even though we know it's AI, it's still so fascinating to us," said Kaiser. "People are adding names and lore to all these AI characters... If a video is viral enough and people like the storyline enough, people just accept it as the new story. [The narrative about the AI generated character] gets spread around, and it becomes official when enough people accept it as official."

Hyperstrides, a 20 year old content creator and student in Los Angeles, said that commentary creators have also played a role in the rise of AI slop storytelling. Commentary creators and podcasters make videos and episodes breaking down the different brain rot storylines, uncovering hidden clues, and predicting where the narratives will go next.

"I think this is definitely a new step in meme and internet culture," Hyperstrides said. "AI has unlocked the possibility to do something extremely creative in a fraction of the time. A lot of creators like me and others [are seeing it]. There's going to be a lot more storytelling. The John Pork story has been one of the most successful AI [stories] that I've seen and I cover a lot of memes. I think because of its success we'll see a lot more people generating their own storylines and lore."

Share

Aidan Walker, a meme historian who publishes the Substack How to Do Things With Memes, said that part of what's driving the popularity of AI storytelling on Reels is young people's desire to go really deep into things. They don't just want a clear cut storyline, they want deep backstories, complicated characters, and shocking twists and turns.

"It's designed to be this sprawling thing," Walker said. "We all know Tim Cheese killed John Pork but everything after that is up for interpretation. You can now get two straight minutes on Bombardiro Crocodilo's relationship with his father."

Walker said that he views these shifts positively. "When AI becomes a thing that we can use to play together and co-create instead of just posting 10,000 slop reels in 24 hours, that's maybe good?" he said.

The shift to generative AI tools undeniably democratizes content creation by letting masses of people contribute to and shape narratives without centralized control. Thousands of users are able to co-create these stories in just minutes, and the lack of centralized power fosters a participatory culture, where audiences are not just consumers but active contributors to the storytelling process.​

The Italian brain rot and John Pork universe is a departure from earlier AI slop storytelling where each story was contained to a single video. For instance, last summer I wrote about how AI-generated cat stories became an overnight phenomenon. The third most viewed video on all of YouTube this week is an AI generated Short of a pug that saves a baby from a plane crash and then landing on an island.

Share

I do think that the long term implications for the future of entertainment are significant. As AI tools become more advanced and accessible, I think we will see more community-driven narratives. This shift could lead to more personalized and immersive storytelling, which reflects a broader range of perspectives and creativity.​

It will also create an IP clusterfuck. Take the John Pork story alone. The real man who created the John Pork character initially gained traction on his account back in 2018. But it was an unaffiliated TikTok user who created the "John Pork is calling" meme, which revived the online character into the public consciousness online in 2023. From there, other random internet users created the basis for the current storyline about Pork's death.

Throughout the story, a real man who calls himself Agent 5.5 has gotten involved as a character, while the rest of the characters in the John Pork universe have been created by a slew of random people online using AI tools. Tim Cheese was created by internet user Choppow in early 2025.

Say someone wanted to create a John Pork universe web series or movie, who owns a collective storyline generated by thousands of internet users, including many children? I think that answers to these questions will become increasingly urgent as entertainment shifts further online and generative AI tools become more pervasive.

Either way, the John Pork and Italian brain rot lore serves as a fascinating case study in how decentralized, AI-assisted storytelling is captivating users and redefining the boundaries of what we consider entertainment online.
